title: Transmission Lines
description: Characteristic impedance, velocity factor, reflections and SWR, stubs, matching and the Smith chart.

study.title: When a line is a transmission line
study.body: A transmission line guides a wave along two conductors: **coax** (unbalanced, shielded), **twin-lead** and twisted pair (balanced), **microstrip** (PCB trace over a ground plane) and **stripline** (trace between two ground planes). A short connection simply carries a voltage. Once a pair of conductors is at least about **0.1 λ** long at the signal frequency, it must be treated as a transmission line: the signal travels as a wave, reflects at a mismatched end and arrives shifted in phase.

study.title: Characteristic impedance
study.body: Every metre of line has series inductance $L$ and shunt capacitance $C$. A travelling wave sees the ratio $V/I = Z_0 = \sqrt{L/C}$, which does not depend on the line length. For coax, $Z_0$ follows from the ratio of shield diameter $D$ to inner-conductor diameter $d$ and the dielectric. Common values: 50 Ω (RF, test equipment), 75 Ω (TV, video), 100–120 Ω (twisted pair), 300 Ω (twin-lead).

study.title: Velocity factor, delay and loss
study.body: In a dielectric the wave travels at $v_p = VF\cdot c$ with $VF = 1/\sqrt{\varepsilon_r}$ (solid PE ≈ 0.66, foam ≈ 0.8), so the wavelength on the line is VF times shorter than in air. A line of length $\ell$ delays the signal by $t_d = \ell/v_p$, a phase lag of $360° \cdot f t_d$. Loss is specified in dB per 100 m (or per 100 ft) at a given frequency; it grows linearly with length and rises with frequency.

study.title: Explore: reflections and standing waves
study.body: A load $Z_L \neq Z_0$ reflects part of the incident wave; the reflection coefficient Γ is the ratio of reflected to incident voltage. The two waves add to a **standing wave** whose pattern repeats every λ/2; $V_{max}/V_{min}$ is the standing-wave ratio. For a resistive load, SWR = $Z_L/Z_0$ or $Z_0/Z_L$, whichever is larger than 1. Drag the load: below $Z_0$ the load sits at a voltage minimum, above $Z_0$ at a maximum.

study.title: Reflected power, return loss, mismatch loss
study.body: A fraction $|\Gamma|^2$ of the forward power is reflected; the rest reaches the load. **Return loss** says how weak the reflection is (larger is better), **mismatch loss** how much load power the reflection costs. SWR 1.5 reflects 4 % (RL 14 dB); SWR 2 reflects 11 % (RL 9.5 dB, mismatch loss 0.5 dB). A directional wattmeter reads $P_f$ and $P_r$, which gives the SWR.

study.title: Lines as circuit elements
study.body: A lossless line transforms impedances. A **shorted stub** gives $+jZ_0\tan\beta\ell$: inductive below λ/4, an open circuit at λ/4 (parallel resonance), capacitive between λ/4 and λ/2; an open stub behaves the other way round. A λ/2 line repeats the load, and a **λ/4 transformer** with $Z_0' = \sqrt{Z_{in}Z_L}$ matches two resistances. A **balun** connects a balanced antenna to unbalanced coax.

study.title: The Smith chart
study.body: The Smith chart plots Γ in the complex plane, labelled with the normalised impedance $z = Z/Z_0 = r + jx$. The centre is $z = 1$ (matched), the left end a short, the right end an open; the outer circle $|\Gamma| = 1$ holds pure reactances, inductive in the upper half and capacitive in the lower half. Moving along a lossless line keeps |Γ| (the SWR) constant: the point turns on a circle around the centre, **clockwise toward the generator**, one full turn per λ/2.

steps.title: When is a cable a transmission line?
steps.body: At low frequencies a cable simply carries a voltage from one end to the other. Once its length is a noticeable fraction of a wavelength, the travel time matters: the signal runs along the line as a wave, reflects at a mismatched end and arrives shifted in phase. Rule of thumb: a pair of conductors acts as a transmission line once it is at least **0.1 λ** long.

steps.prompt: A pair of conductors carries a signal of {{f|Hz}}. From what length on must you treat it as a transmission line? Use the 0.1 λ rule with the free-space wavelength.
steps.explanation: $\lambda = c/f$ = 3 × $10^8$ / {{f|Hz}} = {{3e8/f|m}}. The pair is a transmission line from $0.1\lambda$ = **{{0.1*3e8/f|m}}** on; shorter connections behave as ordinary wires.

steps.prompt: Match each line type to its description.
pairs: Unbalanced; the shield encloses the field
PCB trace above one ground plane
PCB trace between two ground planes
steps.explanation: Coax keeps the field between centre conductor and shield, so it is shielded and unbalanced (shield at ground). Twin-lead is a balanced pair, 300 Ω for the classic TV type. Microstrip and stripline are PCB lines; stripline has ground on both sides, so it hardly radiates but is harder to make.

steps.title: Characteristic impedance
steps.body: Each metre of line has series inductance $L$ and shunt capacitance $C$. A wave travelling on the line sees a constant ratio $V/I = Z_0$, whatever the length. Terminate the line in $R_L = Z_0$ and the whole wave is absorbed: the generator then sees $Z_0$ for any line length.

steps.prompt: A cable has {{Lpm|H}} of inductance and {{Cpm|F}} of capacitance per metre. Find its characteristic impedance.
steps.explanation: $Z_0 = \sqrt{L/C}$ = √({{Lpm|H}} / {{Cpm|F}}) = **{{sqrt(Lpm/Cpm)|Ω}}**. The length does not matter: a longer cable has more L and more C in the same ratio.

steps.prompt: A coax has an inner conductor of {{d*1e3}} mm diameter, a shield of {{D*1e3}} mm inner diameter and a dielectric with $\varepsilon_r$ = {{er}}. Find $Z_0$.

steps.title: Velocity factor
steps.body: A wave on a line travels at $v_p = VF\cdot c$. With a dielectric of relative permittivity $\varepsilon_r$ around the conductors, $VF = 1/\sqrt{\varepsilon_r}$: about 0.66 for solid polyethylene, 0.8–0.85 for foam and close to 1 for an air line. Everything that depends on wavelength, such as a λ/4 section, is VF times shorter in the cable than in air.

steps.prompt: You need a λ/4 section at {{f|Hz}}, cut from coax with a dielectric of $\varepsilon_r$ = {{er}}. How long is it physically?
steps.explanation: $VF = 1/\sqrt{\varepsilon_r}$ = 1/√{{er}} = {{VF}}. $\lambda_{line} = VF\cdot c/f$ = {{VF}} × 3 × $10^8$ / {{f|Hz}} = {{VF*3e8/f|m}}, so λ/4 = **{{VF*3e8/f/4|m}}**. In air it would be {{3e8/f/4|m}}.

steps.prompt: Cutting a 50 Ω coax cable in half gives two cables with a characteristic impedance of 25 Ω each.
steps.explanation: False. $Z_0 = \sqrt{L/C}$ uses the inductance and capacitance **per metre**, which do not change when you cut the cable. Each half is still a 50 Ω cable; only its delay and loss halve.

steps.prompt: Which change **raises** the characteristic impedance of a coax cable?
options: A thinner inner conductor with the same shield
A thicker inner conductor with the same shield
steps.explanation: $Z_0 = \frac{138}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_r}}\log_{10}(D/d)$. A thinner inner conductor increases $D/d$ (less capacitance, more inductance per metre), so $Z_0$ rises. A thicker inner conductor or a higher $\varepsilon_r$ lowers $Z_0$; the length has no effect.

steps.prompt: A {{len|m}} cable run has a loss of {{A100}} dB per 100 m at the operating frequency. A transmitter puts {{Pin|W}} into it.

ask.prompt: What is the total cable loss in dB?
ask.explanation: Loss is proportional to length: $A$ = {{A100}} dB/100 m × {{len|m}} = **{{A}} dB**.

ask.prompt: How much power reaches the far end?
ask.explanation: $A$ = {{A100}} × {{len}}/100 = {{A}} dB, so $P_L = P_{in}\cdot10^{-A/10}$ = {{Pin|W}} × 10^(−{{A}}/10) = **{{PL|W}}**. The other {{Pin-PL|W}} heats the cable.

steps.prompt: A time-domain reflectometer (TDR) sends a fast step into a coax with VF = {{VF}}. The echo from a damaged spot returns {{t|s}} after the step. How far away is the damage?
steps.explanation: The echo travels there **and back**: $d = v_p t/2$ = {{VF}} × 3 × $10^8$ × {{t|s}} / 2 = **{{VF*3e8*t/2|m}}**.

steps.prompt: A sine wave of {{f|Hz}} passes through {{len|m}} of cable with VF = {{VF}}.

ask.prompt: Find the time delay of the cable.
By how many degrees does the output lag the input (0–360°)?
ask.explanation: $t_d$ = {{td|s}} and $T = 1/f$ = {{1/f|s}}. $\theta = 360°\cdot t_d/T$ = 360° × {{f*td}} = {{ph}}°, which is **{{mod(ph,360)}}°** after removing whole cycles.

steps.title: Reflection coefficient and SWR
steps.body: A load $Z_L \neq Z_0$ reflects a fraction Γ of the incident voltage. Incident and reflected wave form a standing wave with $SWR = V_{max}/V_{min}$. Γ > 0 (load above $Z_0$) puts a voltage maximum at the load, Γ < 0 a minimum. A matched line has Γ = 0 and SWR 1; an open or short gives |Γ| = 1 and an infinite SWR.

steps.prompt: A {{Z0}} Ω line is terminated in a {{ZL|Ω}} resistor. Find the reflection coefficient Γ (with its sign).
steps.explanation: $\Gamma = \frac{Z_L - Z_0}{Z_L + Z_0}$ = ({{ZL}} − {{Z0}}) / ({{ZL}} + {{Z0}}) = **{{(ZL-Z0)/(ZL+Z0)}}**. A negative Γ means the reflected voltage is inverted (load below $Z_0$).

steps.prompt: A {{Z0}} Ω line feeds a resistive load of {{RL|Ω}}.

ask.prompt: Find the SWR.
ask.explanation: For a resistive load, SWR is the larger impedance over the smaller: SWR = {{max(RL,Z0)}} / {{min(RL,Z0)}} = **{{max(RL/Z0, Z0/RL)}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the magnitude of the reflection coefficient.
What percentage of the forward power is reflected?
ask.explanation: $|\Gamma|$ = {{abs(RL-Z0)}} / {{RL+Z0}} = {{G}}; the reflected fraction is $|\Gamma|^2$ = **{{100*G^2}} %**.

steps.prompt: A directional wattmeter in the feed line reads {{Pf|W}} forward and {{Pr|W}} reflected.

ask.prompt: Find the SWR.
How much power does the load absorb?
ask.explanation: Whatever is not reflected is absorbed: $P_L = P_f - P_r$ = {{Pf}} − {{Pr}} = **{{Pf-Pr|W}}** (lossless line).

steps.prompt: An antenna feed line has an SWR of {{S}}.

ask.prompt: Find the return loss.
Find the mismatch loss.
ask.explanation: $|\Gamma|$ = {{G}}, so the load receives $1 - |\Gamma|^2$ = {{1-G^2}} of the forward power: $ML = -10\log(1-|\Gamma|^2)$ = **{{-10*log10(1-G^2)}} dB**.

ask.prompt: What percentage of the forward power is reflected?

steps.prompt: The graph shows |V| along the line versus the distance from the load. Drag $R_L/Z_0$ until the SWR is {{S}}, with $R_L > Z_0$.
steps.explanation: SWR = $V_{max}/V_{min}$; for a resistive load above $Z_0$ it equals $R_L/Z_0$, so set $R_L/Z_0$ = **{{S}}**. Then Γ = ({{S}} − 1)/({{S}} + 1) = {{(S-1)/(S+1)}}, $V_{max}$ = 1 + Γ = {{1+(S-1)/(S+1)}} and $V_{min}$ = 1 − Γ = {{1-(S-1)/(S+1)}}. With Γ > 0 the load sits at a voltage maximum.

steps.prompt: A 50 Ω line terminated in 100 Ω and the same line terminated in 25 Ω have the same SWR.
steps.explanation: True: 100/50 = 2 and 50/25 = 2. Γ is +1/3 for 100 Ω and −1/3 for 25 Ω, so |Γ| and the SWR are equal. Only the position of the pattern differs: 100 Ω puts a voltage maximum at the load, 25 Ω a minimum (λ/4 further along).

lessons.title: Stubs, matching and the Smith chart

steps.title: Lines as components
steps.body: A lossless line of length ℓ transforms the load impedance. A shorted stub has input impedance $jZ_0\tan(2\pi\ell/\lambda)$: inductive for ℓ < λ/4, an open circuit at λ/4, capacitive between λ/4 and λ/2. An open stub does the opposite: $-jZ_0\cot(2\pi\ell/\lambda)$ is capacitive below λ/4. At UHF and microwave frequencies such stubs replace coils and capacitors.

steps.prompt: Match each lossless line to what the generator sees at its input.
steps.explanation: With $2\pi\ell/\lambda$ = 45° (λ/8): shorted $jZ_0\tan45° = +jZ_0$, open $-jZ_0\cot45° = -jZ_0$. At λ/4 (90°) the tangent is infinite: a shorted stub looks open, an open stub looks shorted. A λ/2 line turns the impedance once around the Smith chart and repeats the load.

steps.prompt: Which graph shows |V| along a line terminated in a **short circuit**? ($d$ = distance from the load.)
steps.explanation: A short forces $V = 0$ at the load, and with |Γ| = 1 the voltage drops to zero every λ/2: $|V| = 2|\sin(2\pi d/\lambda)|$. The pattern with a maximum at the load is the open line, the flat one a matched line, and the one with non-zero minima a partial mismatch (here Γ = −0.5).

steps.prompt: Set the length of a shorted {{Z0}} Ω stub so that its input reactance is {{Xs}} Ω (positive: inductive, negative: capacitive). The orange line marks the target.
steps.explanation: Solve $\tan(2\pi\ell/\lambda) = X_{in}/Z_0$ = {{Xs/Z0}}. The arctangent gives {{atan(Xs/Z0)}} rad (add π when negative), so ℓ/λ = **{{lt}}**. Below λ/4 a shorted stub is inductive, between λ/4 and λ/2 capacitive.

steps.prompt: A resistive load of {{RL|Ω}} is to be fed from a 50 Ω line through a quarter-wave section.

ask.prompt: Which characteristic impedance must the λ/4 section have for a perfect match?
ask.explanation: A λ/4 line transforms $Z_L$ into $Z_0'^2/Z_L$. For 50 Ω at the input: $Z_0' = \sqrt{Z_{in}Z_L}$ = √(50 × {{RL}}) = **{{sqrt(50*RL)|Ω}}**.

ask.prompt: If you use 75 Ω cable for the λ/4 section, what impedance does the 50 Ω line see?
ask.explanation: $Z_{in} = Z_0'^2/Z_L$ = 75² / {{RL}} = **{{75^2/RL|Ω}}** (a perfect match needs {{sqrt(50*RL)|Ω}}).

steps.prompt: A lossless {{Z0}} Ω line is exactly {{0.5-0.25*n}} λ long and terminated in {{ZL|Ω}}. What impedance do you see at its input?
steps.explanation: A λ/2 line repeats the load, because the impedance pattern repeats every λ/2. A λ/4 line inverts it: $Z_{in} = Z_0^2/Z_L$ = {{Z0}}² / {{ZL}} = {{Z0^2/ZL|Ω}}. This line is {{0.5-0.25*n}} λ long, so $Z_{in}$ = **{{if(n, Z0^2/ZL, ZL)|Ω}}**.

steps.prompt: An antenna with $Z_L = R + jX$, where $R$ = {{R}} Ω and $X$ = {{X}} Ω, is fed by 50 Ω coax.

ask.prompt: Find |Γ|.
Find the SWR on the cable.

steps.title: The Smith chart
steps.body: The Smith chart is a map of Γ, labelled in normalised impedance $z = Z/Z_0 = r + jx$. The centre is a perfect match, the left end a short, the right end an open. Circles of constant $r$ touch the right end; the one through the centre is $r = 1$. Inductive impedances lie in the upper half, capacitive ones in the lower half, pure reactances on the outer circle. A line of length ℓ turns the point clockwise (toward the generator) on its SWR circle, a full turn per λ/2.

steps.prompt: The dot marks a load on a Smith chart (grey: outer circle, the $r = 1$ circle and the $x = \pm1$ arcs). What kind of load is it?
steps.explanation: Points **inside** the $r = 1$ circle (the circle through the centre and the open end) have $R > Z_0$; points outside it, toward the short, have $R < Z_0$. The upper half is inductive, the lower half capacitive. The dot is $z$ = {{r}} + j({{xx}}), i.e. {{50*r}} + j({{50*xx}}) Ω on a 50 Ω chart.

steps.prompt: On a lossless line, moving the measuring point a quarter wavelength toward the generator moves the impedance half a turn around the Smith chart.
steps.explanation: True. One full turn is λ/2, so λ/4 is half a turn: the point jumps to the opposite side of its SWR circle. That is the λ/4 transformer: $z$ becomes $1/z$, a short becomes an open.

steps.prompt: A {{P|W}} transmitter feeds a resistive antenna of {{RL|Ω}} through {{len|m}} of 50 Ω coax with {{A100}} dB/100 m loss. Ignore re-reflections at the transmitter.

ask.prompt: How much power does the antenna accept?
ask.explanation: Cable: $A$ = {{A100}} × {{len}}/100 = {{A}} dB, so {{P}} W × 10^(−{{A}}/10) = {{Pf|W}} arrives at the antenna. Γ = ({{RL}} − 50)/({{RL}} + 50) = {{G}}, so the antenna accepts $1 - \Gamma^2$ = {{1-G^2}} of it: **{{Pa|W}}**.

ask.prompt: What is the total loss from transmitter to antenna (cable plus mismatch)?
ask.explanation: Cable loss {{A}} dB plus mismatch loss $-10\log(1-\Gamma^2)$ = {{-10*log10(1-G^2)}} dB (Γ = {{G}}) gives **{{10*log10(P/Pa)}} dB**: {{P|W}} in, {{Pa|W}} accepted.

steps.prompt: A TDR drives a {{Z0}} Ω cable with a 1 V incident step. When the echo from the far-end termination returns, the trace changes by {{G|V}}. What resistance terminates the cable?
steps.explanation: The echo is the reflected wave: Γ = $V_r/V_i$ = {{G}}. Solving $\Gamma = (Z_L - Z_0)/(Z_L + Z_0)$ for $Z_L$: $Z_L = Z_0\frac{1+\Gamma}{1-\Gamma}$ = {{Z0}} × {{1+G}}/{{1-G}} = **{{Z0*(1+G)/(1-G)|Ω}}**. A positive echo means $Z_L > Z_0$, a negative one $Z_L < Z_0$.

steps.prompt: At {{f|Hz}} you want to replace a {{Lw|H}} inductor by a shorted stub of 50 Ω coax with VF = {{VF}}.

ask.prompt: How long must the stub be?
ask.explanation: $X_L = 2\pi fL$ = {{XL|Ω}}. A shorted stub gives $Z_0\tan\beta\ell$, so $\beta\ell = \arctan(X_L/Z_0)$ = arctan({{XL/50}}) = {{bl}} rad. $\lambda_{line}$ = {{VF}} × 3 × $10^8$ / {{f|Hz}} = {{lam|m}}, so $\ell = \lambda_{line}\cdot\beta\ell/2\pi$ = **{{len|m}}**.

ask.prompt: What is its electrical length in degrees?
ask.explanation: $X_L = 2\pi fL$ = {{XL|Ω}}; $\beta\ell = \arctan(X_L/Z_0)$ = arctan({{XL}}/50) = **{{deg(bl)}}°**, i.e. {{deg(bl)/360}} λ.

steps.prompt: A resistive load of {{RL|Ω}} must be matched to 50 Ω coax with a λ/4 section, but only {{Zq}} Ω cable is available for the section.

ask.prompt: What impedance does the 50 Ω line see?
ask.explanation: Ideal would be √(50 × {{RL}}) = {{sqrt(50*RL)|Ω}}. With {{Zq}} Ω: $Z_{in} = Z_0'^2/Z_L$ = {{Zq}}² / {{RL}} = **{{Zin|Ω}}**.

ask.prompt: What SWR remains on the 50 Ω line?
ask.explanation: $Z_{in}$ = {{Zq}}²/{{RL}} = {{Zin|Ω}} (resistive), so SWR = larger/smaller = **{{max(Zin/50, 50/Zin)}}**, compared with {{RL/50}} without the section.

steps.prompt: A coax cable has $Z_0$ = {{Z0}} Ω and a velocity factor of {{VF}}.

ask.prompt: What is its capacitance per metre?
What is its inductance per metre?
ask.explanation: $Z_0 = \sqrt{L/C}$ and $v_p = 1/\sqrt{LC}$ give $L = Z_0/v_p$ = {{Z0}} / ({{vp/1e8}} × $10^8$) = **{{Z0/vp|H}}** per metre.

steps.prompt: On a 50 Ω line with a resistive load you measure $V_{max}$ = {{Vmax|V}} and $V_{min}$ = {{Vmin|V}}, with a voltage **minimum** right at the load. What is the load resistance?
steps.explanation: SWR = $V_{max}/V_{min}$ = {{Vmax/Vmin}}. A voltage minimum at the load means Γ < 0, so $R_L < Z_0$: $R_L = Z_0/SWR$ = 50 / {{Vmax/Vmin}} = **{{50*Vmin/Vmax|Ω}}**. ({{50*Vmax/Vmin|Ω}} would put a maximum at the load; ({{Vmax}} − {{Vmin}})/({{Vmax}} + {{Vmin}}) is |Γ|, not an impedance ratio.)

steps.prompt: Put the steps in order to find the input impedance of a mismatched line with a Smith chart.
items: Draw the SWR circle through $z_L$ around the centre
Rotate clockwise (toward the generator) by ℓ/λ
steps.explanation: The chart works with normalised values, so first divide by $Z_0$ and plot. Along a lossless line |Γ| stays constant, so the impedance moves on the SWR circle; ℓ/λ toward the generator is a clockwise rotation (a full turn per λ/2). Finally convert the normalised result back to ohms.

steps.prompt: A half-wave dipole (balanced, about 73 Ω) is fed directly with 75 Ω coax. What should be added at the feed point, and why?
options: A 1:1 balun, so no current flows back on the outside of the shield
A 4:1 balun, to step 73 Ω up to 300 Ω
A λ/4 section of 75 Ω cable, to match 73 Ω to 75 Ω
Nothing: coax is already a balanced line
steps.explanation: The impedances already match (SWR ≈ 1.03), but coax is **unbalanced** and the dipole is balanced. Without a balun, part of the current returns on the outside of the shield: the feed line radiates and the pattern is distorted. A 1:1 balun forces equal and opposite currents in the two dipole halves.
